extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Shakespeare; textual editors and bibliographers
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evaluative principles for editing, establishing authority, and judging authenticity of Shakespeare's plays and poems, including how to weigh Folio/Quarto sources, diagnose corruptions, and apply emendation and editorial practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority of the First Folio
rubrics_metrics.description: The First Folio is the most important single volume in the history of the text of Shakespeare; for twenty plays it is our sole authority and its supreme value is justified for those works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give the First Folio primary weight especially where it is the sole or principal source; recognize that for the twenty plays unique to the Folio the task of editing is least difficult. Still assess Folio readings in relation to other evidence where available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative value of Quarto and Folio texts
rubrics_metrics.description: In the remaining plays importance is shared, in proportions varying from play to play, with the texts of the Quartos; in some cases the extant Quarto rather than the Folio is the prime authority for the text today.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh Quarto and Folio comparatively on a play-by-play basis; where a Quarto appears to be the prime authority (e.g., because it derives from a playhouse copy), prefer it unless there is clear reason not to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification and weighting of sources
rubrics_metrics.description: The sources available include playhouse copies, Quartos (including 'better' Quartos), reported texts, and possible manuscript sources; the compilers of the Folio probably obtained material from playhouse copies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess each source for reliability (e.g., playhouse copies often reliable; reported texts are suspect). Prefer sources with clear provenance and corroborating evidence, and note when a source is sole or independent authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial duty to establish author's intention
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases where Folio and Quarto represent rival versions it is the duty of the editor to decide from all the accessible data which version has the best claim to represent the author's intention, and to make that a basis to be departed from only in clear cases of corruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base editorial choice on comprehensive evidence; avoid casual eclecticism that creates a patchwork text not representing any stage of the author's work; depart from chosen basis only for clear corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of excessive eclecticism
rubrics_metrics.description: The temptation ... is naturally towards an eclecticism which adopts the reading that seems most plausible in itself, without giving due weight to the general authority of the text chosen as a basis. If carried far, such eclecticism results in a patchwork quite distinct from any version that Shakespeare can have known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit selection of readings from multiple witnesses; give consistent weight to a principal authority rather than stitching together individually plausible readings from varied sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation of variants and editorial provenance
rubrics_metrics.description: The various readings are fairly put in the margin, so that anyone may compare 'em; the New Variorum records not only the first occurrence of a reading, but the names of the chief editors who have adopted it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a critical apparatus showing variants and indicate the source of each reading and which editors adopted them; transparency in provenance is essential for scholarly utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjectural emendation: use and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The conjectural emendation of Shakespeare still goes on, but comparatively few suggestions find general acceptance. Editors have 'indulged their appetite for conjecture at times beyond reasonable bounds.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use conjectural emendation sparingly and with clear justification; distinguish conjectures from readings attested in witnesses and avoid over-confident impositions without evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of textual corruption (manuscript and printing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fundamental causes include the illegibility or ambiguity of the author's original manuscript; errors of the compositor--confusion of words sounding alike, of words looking alike, unconscious substitution of synonyms, mere manual slips; absence of uniform spelling and carelessness in punctuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating variants, consider these mechanistic causes as likely sources of error; prefer readings that best explain how such errors could arise and consult multiple witnesses to resolve ambiguous cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corruptions specific to reported and surreptitious Quartos
rubrics_metrics.description: Defects include omissions and alterations due to lapse of memory on the part of the actors, additions due to the tendency to improvise, omissions due to the reporter's failure to hear or to write quickly enough, garbled paraphrases made up to supply such omissions, and the writing of prose as verse and verse as prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat reported Quartos with caution; diagnose characteristic reporter-errors (omissions, garbling, prose/verse misdivision) and weigh them against other witnesses like playhouse copies or later Folio readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Playhouse alterations and stage practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Cuts, additions, and alterations were made for acting purposes; stage directions were added with or without the assistance of the author; revivals of the play called for revision by the original writer or another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that many textual differences reflect practical theatrical revision rather than authorial corruption; distinguish probable acting cuts/additions from authorial text and indicate editorially where stage practice likely altered the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of stage directions and scenic notes
rubrics_metrics.description: The majority of stage directions in modern editions, except exits and entrances, are due to editors from Rowe onwards, and these unauthorized additions are distinguished in the Tudor edition by brackets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark editorially-supplied or later stage directions (e.g., with brackets); preserve original exits/entrances when attested but indicate later insertions clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation and orthography not authoritative
rubrics_metrics.description: The punctuation of both Quartos and Folio, though by no means without weight, cannot be regarded as having the author's sanction ... All modernized editions re-punctuate with greater or less freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modernize punctuation and spelling for readability while noting that such modernization often does not affect textual authority; editors may re-punctuate according to modern syntax as long as it does not obscure textual evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial responsibility for external apparatus (dramatis personae, acts/scenes)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Folios only eight of the plays had lists of dramatis personæ; Rowe supplied them for the rest. In the Folios the division into acts and scenes is carried out completely in only seventeen cases ... Rowe again completed the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide dramatis personae, a consistent system of acts and scenes, and complete exits/entrances when preparing a modern edition, but document editorial interventions and be accountable for discretionary structural decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of typographical and documentary evidence for dating and priority
rubrics_metrics.description: Typographical evidence (e.g., Pollard and Greg's work) can show that title-pages were set up in succession in a later year and thus correct publication dates; Stationers' Register entries indicate registration and sometimes omission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ bibliographical, typographical, and registry evidence to establish publication dates, priority, and authenticity; explicit documentary proof should override mere title-page assertions when available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for authenticity and authorship attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions of authenticity arise for poems and plays; for some plays there is general agreement that Shakespeare wrote in part in collaboration; verse tests and external evidence (acting records, registration, style) are used to assign authorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine internal stylistic tests (e.g., verse tests), external documentary evidence (registrations, company records), and historical/contextual data to assess authorship and collaboration; present attributions as probabilistic where evidence is inconclusive.
